title: Distributed Idempotency Key Gateway with Redis & SHA-256 Fingerprinting
problemStatement: In distributed microservice environments, network timeouts and automatic client retries can cause non-idempotent HTTP POST endpoints (e.g., payment charges, order submissions) to be executed multiple times, resulting in duplicate billing or double fulfillment. A distributed idempotency middleware must safely intercept requests carrying an Idempotency-Key header, lock processing during in-flight execution, detect payload mutation via cryptographic hashing, and replay cached responses atomically.
useCases: Payment gateway charge processing shielding merchant accounts from double-charges | Order processing pipeline preventing duplicate inventory deductions | Webhook dispatcher guaranteeing once-and-only-once execution of partner callbacks
problemItSolves: Preventing duplicate database writes caused by network blips and automated HTTP retries | Detecting malicious or buggy payload tampering when a client reuses an idempotency key with conflicting bodies | Avoiding race conditions where two simultaneous identical requests arrive concurrently using atomic SETNX locks
recruiterSignal: Deep understanding of HTTP RFC specifications (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header) | Robust concurrency test suite executing 50 concurrent identical requests with zero duplicate executions | Benchmarks proving less than 3ms overhead added to the request-response lifecycle
architecture: Incoming request carries Idempotency-Key; middleware computes SHA-256 fingerprint of method + path + body; executes atomic Redis SETNX with key and IN_PROGRESS status with 120s TTL; if lock fails, checks stored hash: if matching, awaits completion and returns cached response; if hash differs, returns HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity; upon upstream completion, updates Redis key to COMPLETED with serialized response bytes and 24h TTL.
scaleTargets: Throughput: > 12,000 requests/sec with Redis cluster backend | Overhead Latency (p99): < 2.5ms added to incoming request | Concurrency Safety: 100% duplicate prevention under 100 simultaneous concurrent retries
verificationRubric: 1. Run go test -v -run TestSingleExecution: Sends single POST /v1/orders with Idempotency-Key [Order processed successfully returning HTTP 201 Created with cached status in Redis]

2. Execute go test -v -run TestConcurrentRetries: Fires 50 simultaneous identical requests with identical Idempotency-Key in parallel goroutines [Downstream handler executes exactly once; 49 requests receive identical replay response]

3. Run go test -v -run TestMismatchedPayloadRejection: Sends duplicate Idempotency-Key with different payload body [Gateway immediately rejects request with HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity and mismatch error code]

4. Execute wrk -t4 -c100 -d15s http://localhost:8080/v1/orders -s scripts/idempotency_bench.lua: Stresses middleware under sustained concurrent load [Throughput exceeds 8,000 req/sec with p99 latency < 4ms]
5. Run go test -v -run TestTimeoutUnlock: Simulates downstream server crash during IN_PROGRESS state [Lock expires safely according to TTL, allowing subsequent retry to proceed cleanly]
portfolioBulletFormula: Engineered distributed HTTP idempotency gateway in Go using Redis and SHA-256 payload hashing; guaranteed exactly-once semantic execution across [CONCURRENT_REQUESTS] concurrent retries while adding under [LATENCY_OVERHEAD]ms p99 latency.

title: Transactional Outbox Pattern with PostgreSQL CDC & Kafka Publishing
problemStatement: Updating a local database and publishing a message to a broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ) within the same API handler creates a dual-write problem: if the database commits but the broker connection dies, messages are lost; if the broker succeeds but the database transaction rolls back, downstream consumers receive phantom events. The Transactional Outbox pattern guarantees eventual consistency by persisting domain entities and outbound events within the same ACID database transaction, decoupling broker delivery via Change Data Capture (CDC).
useCases: Financial transactions publishing audit events to compliance pipelines | User registration workflows triggering email notifications and analytics streams | E-commerce order placement triggering inventory and shipping microservices
problemItSolves: Eliminating dual-write data inconsistency between relational databases and message brokers | Reading PostgreSQL Write-Ahead Log (WAL) replication slots via CDC to stream events without table polling load | Handling network partitions with Kafka brokers through at-least-once delivery and deduplication IDs
recruiterSignal: Comprehensive understanding of distributed data patterns, ACID isolation, and Kafka producer mechanics | Automated test injecting broker failure, demonstrating zero lost events upon broker reconnection | Benchmark measuring CDC extraction throughput against direct polling approaches
architecture: Application executes transaction writing to orders table and outbox_events table atomically; PostgreSQL logical replication slot decodes WAL mutations; Go CDC consumer service reads replication stream using pglogrepl; batches events and publishes to Apache Kafka with idempotency keys; acknowledges WAL LSN position only after successful Kafka ACK; downstream consumer idempotently processes message.
scaleTargets: Streaming Latency: < 250ms from database commit to Kafka topic availability | Throughput: > 6,000 outbox events/sec streamed without database degradation | Event Durability: Zero event loss during abrupt Kafka or application crashes
verificationRubric: 1. Run docker-compose up -d and go run cmd/worker/main.go: Starts PostgreSQL with wal_level=logical, Kafka, and outbox worker [Worker connects to logical replication slot and logs READY]
2. Execute go test -v -run TestAtomicCommit: Inserts 1,000 orders into database within ACID transactions [Outbox worker extracts and publishes all 1,000 events to Kafka with zero dropped records]
3. Run go test -v -run TestTransactionRollback: Simulates failed business logic triggering database rollback [Outbox table remains clean; zero spurious events published to Kafka]

4. Execute docker stop kafka && insert_orders 500 && docker start kafka: Simulates broker outage during transaction writes [Worker pauses, resumes upon broker recovery, and flushes all 500 events without duplicate LSN advancement]
5. Run go test -bench=. -benchtime=10s: Benchmarks CDC pipeline throughput under sustained database load [Sustains > 4,500 processed events/sec with minimal WAL lag]
portfolioBulletFormula: Implemented Transactional Outbox CDC pipeline in Go using PostgreSQL logical decoding and Apache Kafka; solved dual-write inconsistency to ensure 100% reliable event delivery across [EVENT_VOLUME] transactions/sec during broker downtime.

title: Resilient Webhook Ingestion & Exponential Backoff Delivery Engine
problemStatement: SaaS applications rely heavily on webhooks to notify external customer servers of business events (e.g., Stripe payments, GitHub events). Customer servers are notoriously unreliable: they frequently experience downtime, timeout, or return 500 internal errors. Naive synchronous delivery exhausts server connection pools and drops critical events. A resilient webhook delivery engine queues dispatches into Redis Streams, signs payloads with HMAC-SHA256, enforces jittered exponential backoff, and routes permanently failed deliveries to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).
useCases: B2B SaaS platform delivering real-time webhook events to customer URLs | Payment gateway relaying transaction confirmations to e-commerce storefronts | Continuous integration systems dispatching build completion hooks
problemItSolves: Preventing slow or unresponsive customer servers from consuming outbound HTTP client workers | Verifying webhook authenticity and payload integrity using HMAC-SHA256 signatures and timestamps | Managing graceful retries across 5 attempts (10s, 1m, 10m, 1h, 6h) with jitter before routing to DLQ
recruiterSignal: Production-grade queue architecture utilizing Redis Streams consumer groups and XACK | Comprehensive security implementation defending against replay attacks with timestamp headers | Administrative dashboard/API to inspect failed webhooks and trigger manual replays from DLQ
architecture: Event publisher pushes event to Redis Stream; Worker pool consumes stream in consumer groups; computes HMAC-SHA256 signature using customer secret; executes HTTP POST with 5s timeout; on 2xx, acknowledges message with XACK; on 5xx or timeout, calculates exponential backoff with full jitter and reschedules to delayed queue; after 5 failed attempts, moves event to Dead Letter Queue and logs alert.
scaleTargets: Delivery Throughput: > 3,500 webhooks/sec dispatched across worker cluster | Concurrency: Manage 500 concurrent outbound HTTP requests without memory bloat | DLQ Isolation: 100% of exhausted retries safely routed to DLQ with detailed failure reason
verificationRubric: 1. Run npm test -- tests/webhook_signature.test.ts: Asserts HMAC-SHA256 signature generation and timestamp header verification [All signature validation tests pass with zero timing attacks]
2. Execute npm test -- tests/retry_backoff.test.ts: Tests exponential backoff calculation with jitter over 5 retry stages [Calculated delay intervals fall within expected mathematical jitter bounds]

3. Run node scripts/simulate_faulty_receiver.js & npm run start:worker: Simulates customer server returning HTTP 503 Service Unavailable [Worker catches error, logs retry attempt, and schedules delay according to policy]

4. Execute npm test -- tests/dlq_routing.test.ts: Simulates continuous delivery failure across maximum retry threshold [Message is cleanly removed from active queue and stored in DLQ with HTTP error status and response body]
5. Run curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/dlq/replay/event_456: Triggers manual DLQ replay after simulated receiver recovery [Event re-enters queue, executes successfully, and receives HTTP 200]
portfolioBulletFormula: Built fault-tolerant webhook delivery platform in TypeScript using Redis Streams and HMAC-SHA256 signatures; automated jittered exponential backoff and DLQ routing to deliver [DISPATCH_VOLUME] daily webhooks with [SUCCESS_RATE]% reliability.

title: Ultra-Low Latency Flash Sale Inventory Reservation Engine
problemStatement: During viral e-commerce flash sales, thousands of users attempt to purchase limited inventory (e.g., 500 items) within milliseconds. Relying directly on relational database transactions (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) causes severe lock contention, thread starvation, connection pool exhaustion, and catastrophic database crashes. Handling flash sales requires atomic in-memory inventory deductions in Redis via Lua scripts, optimistic pre-reservations with short TTLs, and asynchronous batch reconciliation with PostgreSQL.
useCases: Ticketing platforms selling out stadium concert seats within 30 seconds | High-demand sneaker drops and limited-edition retail flash sales | Ride-hailing driver dispatch during sudden geographic demand surges
problemItSolves: Eliminating inventory overselling (selling 505 units when only 500 exist) under extreme concurrent load | Preventing database thread lockups by decoupling user checkout spikes from relational database writes | Automatically reclaiming abandoned reservations after a 10-minute payment timeout using Redis keyspace notifications
recruiterSignal: Flawless demonstration of concurrency control using atomic Redis Lua scripting and optimistic locking | K6 load test proving zero overselling under 10,000 simulated concurrent buyer requests | Asynchronous reconciliation worker syncing reservation logs to PostgreSQL in batches
architecture: Client submits purchase request; Go API executes atomic Redis Lua script: checks available stock, decrements counter, creates reservation record with 10-minute TTL; if stock == 0, returns sold-out in 1.2ms; if reserved, returns reservation token; client completes payment; background sync worker flushes completed reservations to PostgreSQL orders and inventory tables; expired reservations automatically increment stock.
scaleTargets: Peak Concurrency: > 15,000 requests/sec with Redis single-instance Lua execution | Latency (p99): < 4ms per reservation request | Consistency: Exactly 0 over-allocations across 100,000 concurrent attempts on 500 items
verificationRubric: 1. Run redis-cli EVAL "$(cat scripts/reserve.lua)" 1 item_101 user_1 1: Tests atomic Lua reservation script execution [Successfully decrements stock from 500 to 499 and returns reservation UUID]

2. Execute k6 run --vus 500 --duration 10s scripts/flash_sale_load.js: Fires 500 concurrent users against inventory of exactly 100 units [Exactly 100 requests return HTTP 200; remaining requests return HTTP 409 Sold Out; zero overselling]

3. Run go test -v -run TestReservationExpiration: Creates 10 reservations, waits for TTL timeout without payment confirmation [Keyspace expiration handler triggers, restoring inventory stock back to original count]
4. Execute go test -v -run TestPostgresReconciliation: Flushes 1,000 completed Redis reservations to PostgreSQL [All 1,000 rows inserted with matching foreign keys and balance verification]
5. Run redis-benchmark -t eval -q: Measures raw Lua script execution rate on target hardware [Records > 20,000 evaluations/sec with zero script timeout errors]
portfolioBulletFormula: Designed high-concurrency flash sale inventory reservation system in Go using Redis Lua scripts; eliminated lock contention and prevented overselling under [CONCURRENT_USERS] concurrent users while maintaining sub-[P99_LATENCY]ms p99 latency.

title: Multi-Region URL Shortener with Distributed K-Sortable ID Generator
problemStatement: Building a global URL shortener requires generating unique, collision-free, short alphanumeric slugs (Base62) without relying on centralized database auto-increment sequences which form a single point of failure and bottleneck across multi-region deployments. Implementing a distributed 64-bit K-sortable ID generator (Snowflake/Sonyflake variant) combined with multi-tier caching delivers globally unique IDs with sub-millisecond redirection performance.
useCases: High-volume link shortener and link branding platform (Bitly alternative) | Short link generator for transactional SMS marketing campaigns | Compact primary key generator for globally distributed microservices
problemItSolves: Generating globally unique, time-ordered 64-bit IDs without central database roundtrips | Encoding 64-bit integers into compact 7-character Base62 alphanumeric slugs (e.g., `https://sho.rt/7bX9q1Z`) | Caching hot URLs in Redis with Bloom filter pre-checks to eliminate database hits for non-existent slugs
recruiterSignal: Comprehensive understanding of distributed unique ID generation (timestamp, worker ID, sequence bits) | Benchmark proving clock-skew protection and zero collision generation across multiple worker nodes | Production HTTP redirect server responding with HTTP 301/302 and analytics tracking
architecture: Worker node initializes with unique WorkerID; incoming POST /shorten generates 64-bit Snowflake ID (timestamp + node ID + sequence); converts integer to Base62 string; saves mapping to PostgreSQL and Redis; incoming GET /{slug} checks Bloom filter: if absent, returns 404 in 0.5ms; if present, checks Redis cache; if miss, fetches from PostgreSQL and populates cache; increments click metrics asynchronously.
scaleTargets: ID Generation Speed: > 250,000 unique IDs/sec per node | Redirection Latency (p99): < 3ms for cached URLs | Slug Capacity: Over 3.5 trillion unique 7-character Base62 combinations
verificationRubric: 1. Run go test -v -run TestSnowflakeCollisions: Spawns 10 parallel worker instances generating 100,000 IDs each [Zero duplicate ID collisions across 1,000,000 generated identifiers]

2. Execute go test -v -run TestClockDriftHandling: Simulates system clock drifting backwards by 50ms during ID generation [ID generator pauses safely and resumes without generating duplicate or backwards timestamps]
3. Run go test -v -run TestBase62Encoding: Tests bidirectional conversion of 64-bit integers to Base62 strings and back [100% round-trip parity verified across boundary integers 0, 2^32, and 2^63-1]
4. Execute wrk -t4 -c200 -d15s http://localhost:8080/7bX9q1Z: Benchmarks GET redirection endpoint against cached URL [Maintains throughput > 15,000 req/sec with p95 response time < 2ms]
5. Run curl -I http://localhost:8080/non_existent_slug: Queries non-existent link rejected by Bloom filter [Returns HTTP 404 Not Found without issuing SQL query to PostgreSQL database]
portfolioBulletFormula: Developed distributed URL shortening service in Go using 64-bit Snowflake ID generation and Base62 encoding; scaled link redirection to [REDIRECT_THROUGHPUT] req/sec with sub-[LATENCY]ms latency and zero ID collisions across [NODE_COUNT] nodes.

title: Real-Time WebSocket & SSE Pub/Sub Fanout Broadcaster
problemStatement: Delivering real-time events (live sports scores, stock tickers, collaborative cursors) to tens of thousands of concurrent client browsers over WebSockets or Server-Sent Events (SSE) overwhelms single-node servers due to connection memory overhead and goroutine scheduling. Distributing connections across multiple backend nodes requires a high-performance fanout layer using Redis Pub/Sub, efficient binary framing, and heartbeat ping/pong connection reaping.
useCases: Live sports score updates and commentary streaming to web and mobile clients | Financial market real-time price tick distribution | In-app collaborative notification center and live user presence
problemItSolves: Fanning out a single inbound event to 50,000 connected client sockets without quadratic latency degradation | Automatically detecting and reaping dead/zombie client connections via heartbeat ping/pong timers | Supporting both bidirectional WebSockets and lightweight unidirectional Server-Sent Events (SSE)
recruiterSignal: Mastery of low-level networking, Linux epoll/kqueue connection scaling, and OS file descriptor tuning | Load test demonstrating 20,000 concurrent idle WebSocket connections on a single low-memory instance | Detailed memory profiling showing < 10KB RAM consumption per active connection
architecture: Clients establish WebSocket or SSE connection on Go edge nodes; Node registers client connection in local memory bucket; Edge nodes subscribe to Redis Pub/Sub channel; when admin publishes event to channel, all edge nodes receive payload and broadcast asynchronously across active client connections using worker pools; heartbeat loop reaps disconnected clients.
scaleTargets: Concurrent Connections: > 30,000 concurrent active WebSocket connections per node | Fanout Latency: Broadcast message to 10,000 clients in < 45ms | Memory Footprint: < 8KB RAM per active connected client socket
verificationRubric: 1. Run go test -v -run TestWebSocketHandshake: Connects client and validates RFC 6455 protocol handshake and header upgrade [Returns HTTP 101 Switching Protocols with valid Sec-WebSocket-Accept]

2. Execute python load_test_connections.py --clients 10000: Establishes 10,000 concurrent idle WebSocket connections to local server [All 10,000 connections established successfully without socket exhaustion]
3. Run redis-cli PUBLISH sports_scores '{"match_id": 1, "score": "2-1"}': Publishes message to Redis channel [Logs verify instant broadcast delivery across all connected clients in < 50ms]
4. Execute go test -v -run TestHeartbeatReaping: Simulates dead client stopping ping response [Server detects missing pong within 30s heartbeat window and terminates connection file descriptor]

5. Run curl -N -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' http://localhost:8080/events: Validates Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming format [Streams text/event-stream data frames with valid event and data fields]
portfolioBulletFormula: Engineered real-time Pub/Sub fanout broadcaster in Go using Redis and WebSockets/SSE; scaled infrastructure to sustain [CONCURRENT_SOCKETS] concurrent client connections with sub-[FANOUT_LATENCY]ms broadcast fanout across nodes.

title: Distributed Saga Pattern Orchestrator for Microservices Transactions
problemStatement: In microservice architectures, business workflows (e.g., flight booking + hotel reservation + car rental) span multiple independent service databases where traditional two-phase commit (2PC) transactions are too slow, brittle, and create blocking lock dependencies. Implementing an Orchestrated Saga coordinates distributed multi-step transactions via an explicit state machine, automatically triggering backward compensating actions (refunds, cancellations) when any step in the workflow fails.
useCases: Travel booking platforms reserving flight, hotel, and rental car across third-party APIs | E-commerce checkout coordinating inventory reservation, payment charging, and parcel shipping | Financial fund transfers moving money between checking, currency exchange, and foreign accounts
problemItSolves: Maintaining eventual consistency across isolated microservice databases without distributed locking | Executing deterministic compensation workflows in reverse order upon downstream service failures | Persisting saga state to PostgreSQL to survive orchestrator process crashes and resume mid-flight workflows
recruiterSignal: Comprehensive understanding of the Saga pattern, distributed consistency, and idempotency guarantees | Chaos test deliberately killing third-party payment service and proving 100% compensation execution | Visual state machine visualization exportable as Mermaid diagrams
architecture: Order submitted -> Saga Orchestrator initializes state in PostgreSQL; Step 1: Executes ReserveInventory; Step 2: Executes AuthorizePayment; Step 3: Executes DispatchShipment; if Step 3 fails, orchestrator reverses progress: executes RefundPayment -> executes ReleaseInventory; records audit trail; marks saga COMPENSATED.
scaleTargets: Workflow Execution Speed: Process 3-step saga in < 120ms under normal conditions | Crash Resilience: 100% recovery of pending sagas upon orchestrator restart | Compensation Accuracy: Exactly 0 uncompensated stranded reservations across 500 injected failures
verificationRubric: 1. Run npm test -- tests/saga_happy_path.test.ts: Executes complete 3-step order booking workflow [All 3 steps execute in order and saga status transitions to COMPLETED]

2. Execute npm test -- tests/saga_payment_failure.test.ts: Injects payment card decline error at Step 2 [Orchestrator halts forward execution, triggers inventory release compensation, and logs COMPENSATED]

3. Run npm test -- tests/orchestrator_crash_recovery.test.ts: Halts orchestrator process mid-workflow, restarts service [Orchestrator reads uncompleted sagas from PostgreSQL and successfully completes or compensates]
4. Execute npm test -- tests/compensation_idempotency.test.ts: Simulates network retry on compensation handlers [Compensation actions execute idempotently without double-refunding]
5. Run node scripts/export_saga_mermaid.js: Generates state diagram of saga lifecycle [Outputs valid Mermaid.js diagram illustrating all forward states and compensation transitions]
portfolioBulletFormula: Architected distributed Saga transaction orchestrator in TypeScript with PostgreSQL state persistence; coordinated multi-service workflows with automated backward compensation, ensuring 100% data consistency across [TRANSACTION_COUNT] simulated service failures.

title: High-Performance gRPC Microservice Mesh with Client-Side Load Balancing
problemStatement: JSON-over-HTTP/1.1 microservice communication introduces severe latency, high CPU serialization overhead, and lack of type-safe API contracts across teams. Migrating internal inter-service communication to gRPC using Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2 multiplexing drastically improves throughput, but requires robust client-side resilience patterns: round-robin load balancing across healthy replicas, circuit breaking to prevent cascading failures, and deadline propagation to stop wasted compute.
useCases: Internal inter-service RPC communication in high-scale microservice architectures | Low-latency telemetry and metrics streaming from edge nodes to ingestion gateways | Type-safe multi-language backend service contracts
problemItSolves: Replacing verbose JSON payloads with compact binary Protocol Buffers (reducing wire size by up to 70%) | Multiplexing hundreds of concurrent RPC calls over a single persistent TCP connection | Stopping cascading outages across service chains by enforcing gRPC deadlines and circuit breakers
recruiterSignal: Production Protocol Buffers (.proto) definitions with backward-compatible schema evolution practices | Resilience test suite demonstrating circuit breaker opening upon replica failure and auto-recovery | Benchmarks comparing HTTP/1.1 JSON vs gRPC Proto wire size and throughput
architecture: Client service uses gRPC resolver to discover upstream replica IPs; Client-side load balancer distributes RPC calls using round-robin; Sony/gobreaker wraps client stubs; if replica error rate exceeds 50%, circuit breaker trips to OPEN, failing fast without network calls; Context deadlines propagate down the call chain; upstream cancels downstream processing when client drops.
scaleTargets: RPC Throughput: > 25,000 RPC calls/sec per node | Latency Reduction: > 60% latency reduction compared to equivalent HTTP/1.1 JSON APIs | Fail-Fast Response: Trip circuit breaker in < 50ms upon upstream replica crash
verificationRubric: 1. Run protoc --go_out=. --go-grpc_out=. proto/payment.proto: Compiles Protocol Buffer contract into Go stubs [Generates clean Go interfaces with zero compilation warnings]

2. Execute ghz --insecure --proto=proto/payment.proto --call=PaymentService.ProcessPayment -c 50 -n 10000 127.0.0.1:50051: Benchmarks gRPC server throughput [Maintains > 20,000 req/sec with p99 latency < 3ms]
3. Run go test -v -run TestCircuitBreakerTripping: Simulates 60% failure rate from backend server replica [Circuit breaker opens, immediately returns ErrCircuitOpen without executing network call]
4. Execute go test -v -run TestDeadlinePropagation: Sets 50ms context deadline on multi-hop RPC where hop 2 takes 200ms [Hop 2 aborts computation immediately upon deadline expiry, saving CPU cycles]
5. Run go test -v -run TestClientLoadBalancing: Deploys 3 backend replicas and sends 300 RPC requests [Requests distributed evenly across all 3 backend replicas (100 requests each +/- 5%)]
portfolioBulletFormula: Implemented high-throughput gRPC microservice mesh in Go with client-side load balancing and circuit breaking; increased inter-service throughput by [THROUGHPUT_INCREASE]% and reduced network payload size by [PAYLOAD_REDUCTION]% compared to REST/JSON.

title: Dynamic Feature Flag & Experimentation Engine with Hash Ring Bucketing
problemStatement: Hardcoding feature rollouts and configuration toggles requires slow code deployments, preventing fast rollbacks during outages and blocking continuous canary testing. Commercial feature flag platforms (LaunchDarkly) are expensive and introduce third-party network dependencies. A self-hosted feature flag and A/B testing engine evaluates rules locally in memory using deterministic hashing (MurmurHash3), updating rules in real-time across fleet instances via Server-Sent Events (SSE).
useCases: Gradual percentage rollouts (1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%) of risky backend changes | Targeted user targeting based on country, email domain, or subscription tier | Instant kill switch deactivating broken features in < 500ms across all running instances
problemItSolves: Eliminating runtime network RPC calls for flag evaluation by caching rulesets in local RAM | Ensuring deterministic user bucketing across sessions using consistent MurmurHash3 hashing | Streaming real-time rule updates to thousands of client applications in sub-second latency
recruiterSignal: Sub-microsecond local evaluation benchmark proving zero overhead in hot application paths | Statistical uniformity test proving exact percentage bucketing across 100,000 simulated user IDs | Clean management API supporting multi-environment toggles (dev, staging, prod)
architecture: Engine caches feature definitions in local memory sync.Map; Server-Sent Events (SSE) listener receives real-time rule updates from Redis Pub/Sub; IsFeatureEnabled(flagKey, userContext) evaluates targeting attributes; computes MurmurHash3(userId + salt) % 100: if hash < rolloutPercentage, returns true; logs evaluation metric asynchronously.
scaleTargets: Evaluation Latency: < 2 microseconds (0.002ms) per in-memory evaluation | Rule Sync Latency: Propagate flag toggle to 100 server instances in < 350ms | Distribution Accuracy: Flag allocation within 0.2% variance on 50% rollout across 100,000 users
verificationRubric: 1. Run go test -v -run TestDeterministicBucketing: Evaluates same user ID 1,000 times across varying processes [User receives identical bucket assignment 100% of the time without divergence]
2. Execute go test -v -run TestPercentageDistribution: Evaluates 100,000 random user IDs on a 30% rollout rule [Allocates between 29.8% and 30.2% of users to enabled bucket]
3. Run go test -bench=. -benchmem: Benchmarks single-thread and concurrent flag evaluation speed [Reports < 1.5 microseconds per evaluation with zero heap allocations]
4. Execute go test -v -run TestRulePropagation: Updates flag rule in Redis and measures update time on worker node [Worker node updates in-memory rule cache within 200ms via SSE]
5. Run curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/flags/checkout_v2/kill: Triggers global emergency kill switch [Flag immediately evaluates to FALSE for 100% of incoming users]
portfolioBulletFormula: Created low-latency feature flagging and experimentation engine in Go using MurmurHash3 deterministic bucketing; achieved sub-[EVAL_LATENCY] microsecond in-memory evaluations while supporting real-time flag rollouts across [INSTANCE_COUNT] nodes.

title: Distributed Priority Background Job Scheduler with Fair Queuing
problemStatement: Standard FIFO message queues suffer from priority inversion and tenant starvation: if a single enterprise tenant enqueues 50,000 batch export jobs, all other tenants' high-priority interactive tasks (e.g., password reset emails, invoice generation) are stalled for hours. A distributed background job scheduler must enforce multi-tenant fair queuing, support priority levels (Critical, High, Default, Low), handle scheduled future executions, and recover stranded jobs when worker nodes die.
useCases: Multi-tenant SaaS background processing (email delivery, report exports, webhooks) | Scheduled cron job execution with distributed deduplication locks | Video transcode and asset pipeline queuing with priority tiers
problemItSolves: Preventing single noisy tenants from monopolizing shared background worker capacity via Deficit Round Robin | Scheduling delayed jobs using Redis Sorted Sets with epoch timestamp scores | Reclaiming in-progress jobs from dead workers using heartbeat leases and visibility timeouts
recruiterSignal: Clear understanding of distributed worker architectures, Redis Sorted Sets, and lease locks | Automated crash test verifying stranded job reclamation after worker SIGKILL | Concurrency benchmarks demonstrating balanced throughput across 1,000 simultaneous queues
architecture: Jobs enqueued with priority and tenant ID; Scheduler maintains Redis Sorted Sets: scheduled_jobs (scored by run timestamp) and priority_queues (scored by priority weight); Dispatcher evaluates runnable jobs using weighted fair queuing; Worker acquires job lease with 30s heartbeat TTL; on success, deletes job; if worker dies, heartbeat expires and watchdog re-queues job.
scaleTargets: Throughput: > 7,000 jobs enqueued and dispatched per second | Dispatch Latency: Scheduled jobs trigger within 100ms of target execution timestamp | Fair Queuing: Tenant A cannot starve Tenant B of more than 50% available worker concurrency
verificationRubric: 1. Run go test -v -run TestPriorityOrdering: Enqueues Low, Normal, and Critical priority jobs simultaneously [Worker consumes all Critical jobs first, followed by Normal, then Low]
2. Execute go test -v -run TestFairQueuingStarvation: Enqueues 10,000 jobs for Tenant A and 10 jobs for Tenant B [Tenant B jobs finish within 2 seconds despite massive Tenant A backlog]
3. Run go test -v -run TestDelayedJobScheduling: Enqueues job with run_at = +5 seconds from now [Job remains dormant and triggers within 80ms of target epoch timestamp]

4. Execute go test -v -run TestWorkerHeartbeatReclamation: Starts worker on long job, issues SIGKILL to worker process [Watchdog discovers expired heartbeat lease after 30s and safely returns job to queue for another worker]
5. Run go test -bench=. -benchmem: Benchmarks concurrent enqueue and dequeue operations under 100 worker goroutines [Demonstrates > 6,000 processed jobs/sec with zero race conditions]
portfolioBulletFormula: Built distributed priority job scheduler in Go using Redis Sorted Sets and Deficit Round Robin fair queuing; eliminated tenant starvation across [TENANT_COUNT] tenants while processing [JOB_THROUGHPUT] jobs/sec with crash-safe lease reclamation.
